📋 Executive summary in-progress An investigation demonstrating viva-biofilm's multi-strategy competition capability against a specific, citable published result: Cockx et al. 2024's…

An investigation demonstrating viva-biofilm's multi-strategy competition capability against a specific, citable published result: Cockx et al. 2024's Figure 5, where two bacterial growth strategies (Rate vs Yield) compete over oxygen and the winner flips with seeding density. The engine's per-species kinetics, distributed alternating spawner, and per-strategy population/biomass readbacks (added specifically for this reproduction) are exercised end-to-end using the paper's own Table-K Monod parameters.

Question. Cockx et al. 2024 (PLOS Comp Biol, "Is it selfish to be filamentous in biofilms?") introduce iDynoMiCS 2.0 and demonstrate it on a classic microbial-ecology question: does a Rate Strategist (faster growth, lower yield) or a Yield Strategist (slower growth, higher/more efficient yield) win a head-to-head competition for a single limiting substrate — and does the answer depend on how densely the two strategies are seeded? Can viva-biofilm's Rust + process-bigraph engine, extended with per-species kinetics and a distributed multi-strategy spawner, reproduce that competition and its density-dependence?

🧬 Biology — the mechanism this investigation models Two ways to make a living from the same food: grow fast and wasteful (Rate Strategist), or grow slow and efficient (Yield Strategist). In a well-mixed environment the fast…

Two ways to make a living from the same food: grow fast and wasteful (Rate Strategist), or grow slow and efficient (Yield Strategist). In a well-mixed environment the fast grower usually wins outright. But in a spatially structured biofilm, local crowding and substrate gradients change the calculus — how many neighbors you start with can tip a competition that would otherwise have a clean winner. Cockx et al. 2024 used this RS-vs-YS competition (built on Kreft 2004's classic altruism model) to show iDynoMiCS 2.0 capturing exactly that density sensitivity; this investigation asks whether a from-scratch Rust reimplementation of the same core biofilm loop shows the same qualitative sensitivity.

🔬 Scientific argument 1 for · 0 against viva-biofilm reproduces the RS-vs-YS competition CAPABILITY faithfully (exact Table-K kinetics, distributed density seeding, per-strategy tracking)…

Main claim. viva-biofilm reproduces the RS-vs-YS competition CAPABILITY faithfully (exact Table-K kinetics, distributed density seeding, per-strategy tracking) and shows a genuine density-dependent outcome — RS's dominance shrinks as seeding density rises, the same direction as the paper's high-density YS-favoring trend — though not yet the paper's full non-monotonic flip, honestly attributed to a runtime-budgeted shorter observation horizon rather than a modeling defect.

Evidence for

  • fig5-rs-ys-competition: RS biomass fraction 0.825 -> 0.822 -> 0.766 across n_each=5/10/50 (a ~0.06 spread, monotonic decline with density); both strategies persist at every density (this study).

Caveats

  • Horizon shortened to 4.0 days (96 steps) vs the paper's 21 days (504 steps) for runtime-budget reasons — see the study's fidelity caveats. The paper's low-density YS win and intermediate-density flip were not observed within this shorter window.
  • Single-seed, non-ensemble runs per density; IbM is stochastic, so this is a qualitative demonstration, not a statistical claim.
  • 2D shoving mechanics only (matches the paper's Fig. 5 setup); the paper's separate force-based (FbM) comparison and 10-week extension are out of scope.
  • Only oxygen is modeled as the limiting substrate, matching the paper's simplification for this figure.

ResultAt n_each=5/10/50 (dt=1/24 d, the paper's full 21-day / 504-step horizon), the final RS biomass fraction was 0.382 / 0.539 / 0.619 respectively. The winner REVERSES with seeding density: YS wins outright at low density (RS 0.382), RS wins at intermediate (0.539) and high (0.619) density — a genuine density-dependent winner reversal. RS fraction rises monotonically with density (YS-RS-RS), so we reproduce the paper's low-density-YS and intermediate-density-RS legs but NOT its non-monotonic re-flip back to YS at high density (paper: YS-RS-YS). The time-trajectories show the rate-vs-yield mechanism directly: RS surges early (its rate advantage while oxygen is abundant — n=5 rises to RS 0.71 by day 2) then YS gains as the biofilm matures and becomes oxygen-limited (its yield advantage — n=5 falls to 0.38 by day 21). Both strategies persist at every density; biofilm thickness stays bounded (~10-16 um) under surface-erosion detachment.
InterpretationThis is a substantially stronger reproduction than the earlier shortened (4-day) run, which showed RS dominant at every density with no YS win at all. Two engine fixes made the paper's full 21-day horizon tractable and physical: an O(n) neighbor-grid relaxation, and a CONVERGED reaction-diffusion coupling that makes the Monod oxygen limitation actually bite, so the population self-limits (grows ~linearly, not exponentially to ~10^5 agents). With them, the competition genuinely reproduces the paper's CORE finding — seeding density decides the winner (YS at low density, RS at intermediate/high). It does not reproduce the paper's exact non-monotonic YS-RS-YS shape (we get monotonic YS-RS-RS, missing the high-density re-flip), plausibly because of our 2D single-oxygen simplification vs the paper's fuller multi-substrate/FbM setup and geometry differences — graded honestly as drift on its own non-gating axis, not folded into the passing groups.

Purpose & background (study design)
Question. Cockx et al. 2024 (Fig. 5) report that when a Rate Strategist (RS — faster growth, lower yield) competes against a Yield Strategist (YS — slower growth, higher/more efficient yield) for a single shared oxygen substrate in a 2D biofilm, the winner depends on seeding density: YS is favored at low density, RS at intermediate density, YS favored again at high density. Does viva-biofilm's multi-strategy competition engine — seeded with the paper's exact Table-K RS/YS kinetics — reproduce a density-dependent competition outcome, and in what direction?
